name: Nova Scotia
note: Full Nova Scotia practice-area pack (common-law). the Residential Tenancies Program (Director of Residential Tenancies) for housing, provincial employment standards, the Small Claims Court for money claims (limit $25,000), Nova Scotia Human Rights Commission, family law. Criminal law is federal (core). Verify; not legal advice.

getLawyer.why: Criminal law is federal (Criminal Code); Nova Scotia has its own courts and Nova Scotia Legal Aid. If charged or arrested, say you want a lawyer and stay silent, ask for free duty counsel, and contact a local criminal lawyer through Nova Scotia Legal Aid before any statement.

If child protection authorities remove or threaten to remove a child in Nova Scotia, timelines are short. Get a family/child-protection lawyer and contact Nova Scotia Legal Aid immediately; you have the right to be heard at the first hearing.

deadlines.title: Eviction / tenancy notice — act within the stated period
deadlines.rule: In Nova Scotia, residential tenancy disputes (unpaid rent, eviction, deposits, repairs) are decided by the Residential Tenancies Program (Director of Residential Tenancies). An eviction or termination notice carries a short response/remedy period — don't wait it out. Paying arrears or fixing the breach in time often preserves the tenancy, and you can dispute the notice before the Residential Tenancies Program (Director of Residential Tenancies). Confirm the exact days for your notice type.

deadlines.title: Unpaid wages / termination — file an Employment Standards claim promptly
deadlines.rule: Unpaid wages, overtime, vacation, and termination pay in Nova Scotia are enforced by the provincial/territorial employment standards office. There is a filing time limit (it varies by jurisdiction) — file promptly. Statutory termination notice is a floor; common-law reasonable notice for a without-cause dismissal is often much larger, so get advice before signing a release.

deadlines.title: Human rights complaint — file within the time limit (often 1 year)
deadlines.rule: Discrimination in work, housing, or services can be taken to the Nova Scotia Human Rights Commission. Most Canadian human rights bodies require filing within 1 YEAR of the last incident — confirm the current limit and file promptly.

deadlines.title: Civil lawsuit — generally a 2-year limitation
deadlines.rule: Most Nova Scotia civil claims (debt, contract, negligence, property) must be started within the limitation period — generally 2 YEARS from when you discovered the claim in common-law provinces, with an ultimate longstop. Some claim types differ. Confirm before relying.

statutes.title: Money claims up to $25,000
statutes.summary: The Small Claims Court hears civil money claims up to $25,000 in Nova Scotia; larger claims go to the superior court. Small-claims procedure is streamlined and designed to be used without a lawyer.

statutes.title: Tenancy disputes go to the Residential Tenancies Program (Director of Residential Tenancies)
statutes.summary: Residential tenancy disputes in Nova Scotia — eviction, deposits, repairs, rent — are decided by the Residential Tenancies Program (Director of Residential Tenancies), not the regular courts. Notices carry short response windows; dispute in time and keep written records.

book.title: Renting in Nova Scotia — tenants and landlords
book.overview: Nova Scotia tenancies are governed by provincial/territorial residential-tenancy legislation and decided by the Residential Tenancies Program (Director of Residential Tenancies) (not the regular courts). Eviction and termination notices carry short response windows — read the notice, note the deadline, and dispute or remedy in time.
your_rights: Right to dispute an eviction/termination notice before the tenancy body.
Limits on deposits and on how/when rent can be increased (confirm the local rule).
Right to habitable premises and essential services.
Right to a written record of the tenancy and its condition.
key_steps: Read the notice: identify the type and the exact deadline.
Pay arrears or fix the breach in time where possible.
Apply to the Residential Tenancies Program (Director of Residential Tenancies) to dispute, before the deadline.
Document everything (photos, receipts, written notices).
Get help from Nova Scotia Legal Aid or a local tenant service.
common_mistakes: Waiting out the notice instead of disputing.
Assuming court instead of the tenancy body.
book.when_lawyer: Most tenancy matters don't need a lawyer; get advice for a bad-faith eviction, a large claim, or an appeal.

book.title: Work in Nova Scotia — your rights and termination
book.overview: Employment standards legislation sets Nova Scotia minimums (wages, overtime, vacation, termination), enforced by the provincial/territorial employment standards office. Statutory termination notice is a floor — for a without-cause dismissal, common-law reasonable notice is often much larger, so don't sign a severance release before getting advice.
your_rights: Statutory minimum termination notice/pay that scales with service.
Often much more under common law if dismissed without cause.
Unpaid wages, overtime, and vacation are recoverable.
Protection from reprisal for asserting your rights.
key_steps: Don't sign a severance release right away — get it reviewed.
Compare the statutory minimum with possible common-law notice.
File an employment standards claim promptly for pay issues.
Keep the contract, pay stubs, and termination letter.
For wrongful dismissal above the small-claims limit, consider the superior court.
common_mistakes: Assuming 'at-will' employment (not a thing in Canada).
book.when_lawyer: Before signing severance, or for without-cause/constructive dismissal or discrimination — get an employment lawyer.

book.title: Suing (and being sued) for money in Nova Scotia
book.overview: The Small Claims Court hears money claims up to $25,000 in Nova Scotia; larger claims go to the superior court. A roughly 2-year limitation period usually applies in common-law jurisdictions — confirm yours.
your_rights: Claims up to $25,000 in the streamlined small-claims process.
Right to bring or defend a claim yourself.
Right to a settlement/pre-trial step.
Right to enforce a judgment (garnishment, seizure).
key_steps: Confirm the amount (≤ $25,000 → small claims).
File within the limitation period (generally ~2 years).
Gather contracts, invoices, messages, proof of loss.
Attend the pre-trial/settlement conference.
After winning, use enforcement to collect.
common_mistakes: Filing in the wrong court for the amount.
book.when_lawyer: Small claims is designed to be self-represented; get advice for superior-court claims or complex matters.

book.title: Family law in Nova Scotia — separation, children, support
book.overview: Nova Scotia family law (parenting, support, and property) runs under provincial/territorial legislation; divorce itself is federal. Child and spousal support follow the Guidelines, and parenting is decided on the child's best interests. Many issues can be settled by agreement or mediation.
your_rights: Parenting decided on the child's best interests.
Child and spousal support under the Guidelines.
Property/relationship rights under local family legislation (confirm how common-law partners are treated).
Right to mediation and a written agreement.
key_steps: Get a parenting plan and a written separation agreement.
Exchange full financial disclosure.
Use family mediation where available.
For safety, seek a protection order.
File in the correct court for your issue.
common_mistakes: Assuming common-law partners' rights without checking.
Withholding a child without an order.
book.when_lawyer: For property, relocation, protection orders, or any dispute involving children — get a family lawyer; Nova Scotia Legal Aid may apply.
book.statute: Nova Scotia family legislation; Divorce Act (federal)

book.title: Charged with a crime in Nova Scotia
book.overview: Criminal law is the federal Criminal Code, so your core rights are the same across Canada: to be told the charge, to stay silent, and to a lawyer without delay — including free immediate advice. Nova Scotia has its own courts and Nova Scotia Legal Aid.
your_rights: Right to silence — you don't have to answer questions.
Right to a lawyer without delay, and free immediate advice (duty counsel).
Right to know the charge and to reasonable bail.
Presumption of innocence.
key_steps: Say: 'I want a lawyer and I will remain silent.'
Ask for free duty counsel; contact Nova Scotia Legal Aid.
Don't discuss the case with anyone but your lawyer.
Note officer details and what happened.
Attend every court date; follow release conditions.
common_mistakes: Talking to police without a lawyer.
Assuming a minor charge needs no lawyer.
book.when_lawyer: Immediately on any arrest or charge — free duty counsel first, then a local criminal lawyer; apply to Nova Scotia Legal Aid.
book.statute: Criminal Code (federal); Nova Scotia court rules

book.title: Debt & collections in Nova Scotia
book.overview: If a collection agency is after you, Nova Scotia's consumer-protection rules limit how and when they can contact you — generally no harassment, no threats, limited call hours, and no contacting your employer about the debt (except to confirm employment). You can usually require written contact only. Old debt may be past the limitation period, so it can't be successfully sued on — but making a payment or admitting the debt can restart that clock.
your_rights: Freedom from harassment, threats, and calls at unreasonable hours.
Right to require contact in writing only.
Collectors generally can't discuss your debt with family/employer.
A debt past the limitation period can't be successfully sued on.
key_steps: Ask for details of the debt in writing before paying.
Send a written notice if you want contact limited to writing.
Check whether the debt is past the limitation period (often ~2 years).
Don't make a payment or admission on an old debt without advice.
Complain to your provincial consumer-protection office about an abusive collector.
common_mistakes: Paying to make it stop without confirming the debt is yours and in time.
Restarting the limitation clock by paying a little on an old debt.
Ignoring a court claim (leads to default judgment + garnishment).
book.when_lawyer: If you're sued, facing garnishment, or the debt isn't yours — get advice; Nova Scotia Legal Aid or a community legal clinic may help.

book.title: Injured in an accident in Nova Scotia
book.overview: If you're hurt by someone's carelessness — a car crash, a fall, a defective product — you may have a claim for your losses (treatment, lost income, pain and suffering). The general limitation period is usually 2 years from when you knew of the claim, but there are often MUCH shorter notice deadlines (e.g., for injuries on municipal property or involving a government body). Document everything and get advice early.
your_rights: Right to seek compensation for your injuries and losses.
Right to your own medical care and records.
Right not to give the other insurer a recorded statement.
Right to a lawyer before signing any release.
key_steps: Get medical care and keep all records and receipts.
Photograph the scene and injuries; get witness contacts.
Report it and get any incident/police report number.
Watch for SHORT notice deadlines (municipal/government claims).
Don't sign a release or accept a quick settlement without advice.
common_mistakes: Missing a short notice deadline (e.g., slip-and-fall notice).
Giving the other insurer a recorded statement.
Settling before your injuries are fully known.
book.when_lawyer: For any serious injury, disputed fault, or an insurer lowballing you — get a personal-injury lawyer (usually contingency, free consult).
book.statute: Nova Scotia negligence law; limitation + notice periods

book.title: Traffic tickets & driving offences in Nova Scotia
book.overview: A traffic ticket in Nova Scotia usually lets you plead guilty (pay the fine, take the demerit points, and risk higher insurance) or dispute it. Serious matters — impaired driving, dangerous driving, driving while suspended — are Criminal Code offences with severe, often mandatory penalties, and should be treated like any criminal charge: get a lawyer and don't just plead.
your_rights: Right to dispute a ticket instead of paying.
Right to disclosure of the evidence against you.
Right to a lawyer for any Criminal Code driving charge.
Presumption of innocence on contested charges.
key_steps: Note the deadline to dispute — don't miss it.
Remember paying the ticket = pleading guilty (points + insurance).
For demerit/insurance concerns, consider disputing or a plea discussion.
For impaired/dangerous/suspended driving, get a lawyer immediately.
Never ignore a ticket — it can lead to a suspension or more charges.
common_mistakes: Paying one you could have fought or reduced.
Treating an impaired-driving charge like a parking ticket.
book.when_lawyer: For impaired driving, dangerous driving, driving while suspended, or any accident causing injury — get a lawyer right away.
book.statute: Criminal Code (impaired/dangerous driving); Nova Scotia highway traffic law

book.title: Your rights with police in Nova Scotia
book.overview: Across Canada the Charter protects you: the right to be free from unreasonable search (s.8), the right not to be arbitrarily detained (s.9), and — on arrest or detention — the right to be told why and to speak to a lawyer without delay (s.10). You generally don't have to answer questions. Stay calm, don't resist, assert your rights clearly, and challenge any breach later in court.
your_rights: Right to silence — you don't have to answer questions.
Right, on detention/arrest, to be told why and to call a lawyer without delay.
Protection from unreasonable search and seizure (s.8).
Protection from arbitrary detention (s.9).
key_steps: Ask: 'Am I being detained, or am I free to go?'
Say you wish to speak to a lawyer and will remain silent.
Don't physically resist; keep your hands visible.
Use free 24-hour duty counsel if offered.
Write down what happened and officer details afterward.
common_mistakes: Consenting to a search you could refuse.
Not clearly asserting the right to counsel.
book.when_lawyer: After any arrest, detention, or search — exercise your right to a lawyer right away; free duty counsel is available 24/7.
book.statute: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, ss.8, 9, 10

book.title: Wills & estates in Nova Scotia
book.overview: A will directs who inherits your property and names the executor who administers your estate. Without a valid will you die 'intestate' and Nova Scotia's default rules decide who inherits — often not what you'd choose, and common-law partners may get nothing automatically. After a death the estate is usually 'probated' (the court confirms the will and the executor's authority) before debts are paid and gifts distributed.
your_rights: Right to make a will (signed and properly witnessed) directing your estate.
Right, as executor, to administer the estate (and to compensation).
Beneficiaries' right to an accounting.
Spouses/dependants may have protected claims against an estate.
key_steps: Make a valid will; name an executor, a backup, and a guardian for minor kids.
Keep beneficiary designations (insurance, registered accounts) current — they can bypass the will.
Store the will safely and tell your executor where it is.
After a death, locate the will and apply for probate; inventory assets/debts.
Pay debts and taxes BEFORE distributing — an executor can be personally liable.
common_mistakes: Assuming a common-law partner automatically inherits.
book.when_lawyer: For estate planning, a contested will, a large/insolvent estate, or executor duties — see a wills & estates lawyer; Nova Scotia Legal Aid may help those who qualify.

book.title: Insurance claims & disputes in Nova Scotia
book.overview: Insurers in Nova Scotia owe a duty of good faith — to handle claims fairly and promptly. If a claim is denied or underpaid, demand the reason and policy wording in writing, appeal internally, and escalate to the General Insurance OmbudService (GIO), the provincial regulator, or court. An unreasonable denial can expose the insurer to extra damages.
your_rights: Right to a written reason for a denial and the policy wording.
Right to a fair, prompt investigation (good faith).
Right to the GIO/ombudsperson and the regulator.
Possible extra damages for bad-faith handling.
key_steps: Report the claim promptly and as the policy requires.
Document the loss — photos, receipts, a log of every contact.
Get the denial reason and policy terms in writing.
Appeal in writing, citing the policy.
Escalate to the GIO/regulator or a lawyer if stonewalled.
common_mistakes: Accepting a denial without the written reason.
book.when_lawyer: For a large denied claim, suspected bad faith, or a liability claim against you — consult an insurance lawyer.
book.statute: Nova Scotia insurance law; duty of good faith

book.title: Small business & self-employed in Nova Scotia
book.overview: Running a business in Nova Scotia means picking a structure (sole proprietor = simple but personally liable; corporation = separate entity limiting personal liability), using written contracts, registering/licensing as required, and keeping business and personal finances separate. Put deals in writing, invoice with clear terms, and get advice before signing leases or big contracts.
your_rights: Right to choose a structure that fits your risk.
Right to enforce written contracts and unpaid invoices.
Right to limited liability if you properly incorporate and maintain the company.
Right to sue (small claims within the limit) to collect.
key_steps: Pick sole prop vs incorporation with tax + legal advice.
Use written contracts and clear invoices.
Register the business name and get required licences.
Keep business and personal money separate.
For unpaid invoices, demand then sue within the limitation period.
book.when_lawyer: For incorporation, a shareholder/partnership agreement, a major contract, or a dispute — get a business lawyer.
